files.label: __main__.py
files.summary: One command runs the exam: ask every question, score the answers four ways, log the run, print the numbers.

notes.title: Step 1: ask the system
notes.body: Load the golden set, then send every question to the running W2 API. The system configuration (top_k, reranker, retrieval mode) travels with the request, so one API can be evaluated under many configurations.

notes.title: Step 2: the free scorers
notes.body: Error rate, retrieval metrics, legal checks and the bilingual test are plain Python. No tokens, no randomness. They run first and they run on every commit.

notes.title: Step 3: the paid scorer
notes.body: RAGAS calls an LLM judge for every question and metric. --skip-ragas exists so you can iterate on retrieval for free and only pay for the judge when it matters.

notes.title: Step 4: record what you tested
notes.body: Everything that could change a score is a parameter: system config, judge model, number of questions, and a hash of the golden set. Two runs are only comparable if these match.

notes.title: Step 5: log it
notes.body: One MLflow run per evaluation, plus report.json on disk for the CI gate to read.

notes.title: The gate command
notes.body: python -m evaluation gate report.json exits 1 if any threshold breaks. That exit code is the whole interface to CI in Workshop 5.

files.label: golden_set.py
files.summary: The golden set schema. Pydantic validates every record before a single token is spent.

notes.title: Question types are part of the schema
notes.body: Every question is tagged with what it tests. This lets you report scores per type: a system can ace lookups and fail every repealed article, and the average hides it.

notes.title: One record
notes.body: gold_articles is what makes legal RAG easy to evaluate: the right answer rests on article numbers, so retrieval can be scored by ID match. pair_id links the Arabic and English versions of the same question.

notes.title: Validation catches bad exam questions
notes.body: A question with no gold articles silently scores 0 on retrieval forever. The validator makes that a loud error unless the question is out of scope on purpose.

notes.title: Loading
notes.body: JSONL: one record per line, easy to diff in a PR. limit is how we keep the room to 20 questions.

notes.title: Fingerprint
notes.body: A short hash of the file, logged with every run. If someone edits the golden set, old and new scores are no longer comparable, and MLflow shows it.

files.label: client.py
files.summary: The only place the evaluator touches the RAG system. Swap it to evaluate any implementation.

notes.title: Contexts, not just citations
notes.body: RAGAS needs the article text the generator actually saw. The W2 response must expose it: design your API to be evaluable.

notes.title: A protocol, not a dependency
notes.body: The evaluator depends on this one method. An in-process client, an HTTP client or a fake for tests all fit.

notes.title: HTTP client for /ask
notes.body: Adds return_contexts plus the experiment options to every request and validates the response shape. Adapt here when the W2 API contract changes.

files.label: runner.py
files.summary: Asks every golden question with bounded concurrency and keeps everything the system returned.

notes.title: A record is the unit of evaluation
notes.body: Question, answer, contexts, latency, error and a scores dict that each scorer fills in. Keeping per-question scores is what lets you answer why a number moved.

notes.title: Article IDs in rank order
notes.body: Retrieval metrics only need this list. Rank order matters for MRR and nDCG.

notes.title: Bounded concurrency
notes.body: Four requests at a time: fast enough, and it will not trip the LLM provider's rate limit with a shared workshop key.

notes.title: Failures are data
notes.body: One timeout must not kill a 20-minute run. Errors are recorded per question and reported as error_rate, which the gate caps at zero.

files.label: retrieval_metrics.py
files.summary: Classic IR metrics on article IDs. No LLM involved.

notes.title: hit@k
notes.body: Did at least one gold article make the top k? The bluntest and most useful number for a lookup question.

notes.title: recall@k
notes.body: What fraction of the needed articles made the top k. This is what drops on multi-article questions.

notes.title: precision@k
notes.body: What fraction of the top k is useful. Low precision means the generator reads noise, which costs tokens and invites confusion.

notes.title: MRR
notes.body: 1 / rank of the first gold article. Rewards putting the right article first, which is what the reranker is for.

notes.title: nDCG@k
notes.body: Rank-weighted gain divided by the best possible ordering. 1.0 means every gold article is at the top.

notes.title: Per question, then the mean
notes.body: Scores go into each record first, then get averaged. Out-of-scope questions have no gold articles, so they are skipped instead of counted as zero.

files.label: legal_checks.py
files.summary: Rules a lawyer would check first. Plain regex, because a citation is right or wrong.

notes.title: Patterns for both languages
notes.body: Arabic-Indic digits (١٤٧) are normalised to 147. The citation pattern covers المادة, للمادة, Article and Art.

notes.title: Which articles did the answer cite?
notes.body: cited_articles("وفقاً للمادة ١٤٧") returns {147}. Everything below builds on this set.

notes.title: Phantom citations
notes.body: Cited articles must be a subset of retrieved articles. An article the model never saw came from its memory: in law that is the most dangerous kind of answer.

notes.title: Repealed and out of scope
notes.body: For a repealed article the only correct answer says so. For a criminal-law question the correct answer is a refusal. These are behaviours, so they get their own metrics.

notes.title: Not applicable is not zero
notes.body: None means the check does not apply to this question. Counting it as 0 would quietly drag every average down.

files.label: bilingual.py
files.summary: Same question in Arabic and English: do we retrieve the same articles?

notes.title: Group by pair_id
notes.body: Every question exists in both languages, linked by pair_id. Pairs where either side errored are dropped.

notes.title: Agreement
notes.body: Top-1 agreement and Jaccard overlap of the top k. A good multilingual embedder gives nearly identical lists.

notes.title: The headline number
notes.body: Negative means Arabic retrieval is worse than English on the same questions. That gap is invisible if you only test in one language.

files.label: ragas_eval.py
files.summary: The four RAGAS metrics, using the ragas 0.4 metrics.collections API and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

notes.title: The judge is its own model choice
notes.body: Same LLM_BASE_URL as the generator, but JUDGE_MODEL can differ. Prefer a different model family from the generator to reduce self-preference bias, and log it: a new judge means new scores.

notes.title: Four metrics, two sides
notes.body: Faithfulness and answer relevancy judge the generator. Context precision and recall judge the retriever, using the reference answer. Answer relevancy also needs embeddings: a multilingual model, because questions are Arabic.

notes.title: Each metric reads different fields
notes.body: Faithfulness never sees the reference. Context recall never sees the answer. Knowing the inputs tells you what a metric can and cannot catch.

notes.title: A judge failure is unknown, not zero
notes.body: Judges time out and return malformed JSON. Recording None keeps a flaky judge from looking like a bad system.

notes.title: Skip what does not apply
notes.body: Out-of-scope questions have no supporting articles, so context metrics are meaningless for them. Their correctness is checked by refused_out_of_scope instead.

files.label: tracking.py
files.summary: Each evaluation becomes an MLflow run you can compare, with the per-question file attached.

notes.title: The file you open when a score drops
notes.body: One row per question with its scores and answer. Averages tell you that something broke; this file tells you which question and why.

notes.title: Files first
notes.body: report.json is written before MLflow is touched, so the CI gate still works if the tracking server is down.

notes.title: Params, metrics, tags
notes.body: Params are what you changed. Metrics are what you got. Tags hold the git SHA and golden-set hash so any number can be traced back to exact code and exact questions.

files.label: gate.py
files.summary: Reads report.json and thresholds.toml, prints failures, exits 0 or 1.

notes.title: Silent metrics fail
notes.body: If a scorer crashed and a metric is missing, the gate fails. A gate that passes when it cannot see is decoration.

notes.title: Absolute floors
notes.body: Faithfulness must stay above 0.75, whatever the baseline. This is the line no PR may cross.

notes.anchor: elif baseline and name in baseline
notes.title: Regression vs main
notes.body: Also fail when a metric drops more than max_drop below the main branch, even if still above the floor. Slow decay is caught one PR at a time.

notes.title: The exit code is the interface
notes.body: CI only understands exit codes. Workshop 5 wires this into GitHub Actions so a red gate blocks the merge.

notes.title: Stable id
notes.body: Never reuse an id. Per-question results are compared across runs by id.

notes.title: Written like a real user
notes.body: Avoid copying the article's wording into the question: that makes BM25 look brilliant and tests nothing.

notes.title: Language
notes.body: Lets you report every metric for Arabic and English separately.

notes.title: What it tests
notes.body: repealed: the correct answer is that Article 60 has no text in force. A system that answers it confidently fails, however fluent it sounds.

notes.title: Reference answer
notes.body: Written or approved by a lawyer. Context precision and recall compare against it. Faithfulness does not use it.

notes.title: Gold articles
notes.body: The article numbers a correct answer must rest on. These make retrieval scoring free and deterministic.

notes.title: Bilingual pair
notes.body: Links this question to its English twin, q007-en, for the bilingual ablation.
